findings.claim: AutoHDR accepts any number of brackets per angle, from 1 up to about 10, but recommends 3. It says quality gains level off after 3.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: AutoHDR accepts any number of brackets — one, two, three, or as many as ten... There are diminishing returns in quality after three brackets... Three brackets gives you faster shooting on-site and faster uploads with no quality loss.

findings.claim: There is no cap on brackets per listing. A single upload can mix 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 brackets per angle with aerials, interiors and exteriors.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: As many as you want. ... whether it's 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9 brackets per angle and any mix of aerials, interiors, and exteriors can go in one upload.

findings.claim: The FAQ says 3 brackets at ±2 EV is enough for most shoots. It suggests 5 only for very bright or sunny markets (Florida, California, desert climates), where 3 may not be dark enough to show window views.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: 3 brackets at ±2 EV is all you need for most shoots ... very bright or sunny markets (Florida, California, desert climates) ... Start with 3. If your window views aren't coming through the way you want, try 5.

findings.claim: The pipeline is built around 3 input frames. When more than 3 brackets are uploaded (for example 5), the AI picks the 3 it judges will give the cleanest, most natural output for that angle.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: when you upload 5, the AI picks the 3 that produce the cleanest, most natural-looking output for that angle ... extra brackets serve as options rather than being discarded.

findings.claim: The fusion model most likely takes a fixed 3-frame input, so there is a separate frame-selection step before it. Given the stated roles of the 3 frames (dark for windows, mid for color, bright for shadows), selection is probably based on exposure coverage, for example the darkest frame that still shows window detail.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Inference from: 'pipeline is built around three-bracket processing' and the role description on brackets-for-handheld-real-estate (dark/bright/mid).

findings.claim: AutoHDR gives each of the 3 brackets a role: the dark frame captures the window view, the bright frame captures shadow detail, and the mid frame gives neutral exposure and the color reference.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Dark bracket — captures the view outside the window; Bright bracket — captures detail in dark parts of the room; Mid bracket — provides neutral exposure and color reference.

findings.claim: Recommended spacing is at least 2 stops (±2 EV) between brackets. The FAQ says 1 EV spacing is too narrow and can make the blend look flat or washed out.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: If your brackets are only 1 EV apart, the AI has a narrow range to work with and the blend can look flat or washed out. 2 EV apart at 3 brackets gives better results.

findings.claim: The official shooting recipe is JPEG with at least 3 brackets at ±2 EV. The knowledge base says to shoot 3 or 5 bracketed exposures per angle at ±2 EV, quickly, and without moving the camera.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Shoot 3 or 5 bracketed exposures per angle at ±2 EV apart ... A tripod helps with alignment but is not required, handheld photography works well as long as brackets are taken in quick succession.

findings.claim: Window-pull quality is capped by the darkest bracket: AutoHDR can only produce a window view as good as the one in the darkest frame. If that frame's windows are blown out, the blend carries the blown-out windows through.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: AutoHDR can create a window view only as good as the window view in your darkest bracket ... make sure the lowest exposure is dark enough that the outside is visible.

findings.claim: For exterior sky and roof boundaries, at least one bracket needs visible sky detail. Without it, sky replacement can bleed into the roof. Already-delivered images with this problem are fixed manually after an email to delivery@autohdr.com.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Keep at least one bracket with visible sky detail ... Send the affected image to delivery@autohdr.com and we'll get it fixed so you can deliver on time.

findings.claim: A tripod is not required. AutoHDR aligns handheld brackets that don't overlap perfectly, but it cannot remove motion blur within a single exposure.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Blur from shake during a single exposure stays in the output, because the AI aligns frames but cannot sharpen motion blur in the source.

findings.claim: Ghosting or transparency across a whole shoot means the camera moved substantially between frames, which alignment cannot fix. The suggested repair is an AI Re-Edit prompt; for future shoots, use a tripod.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Use AI Re-Edit on affected photos with a prompt like "remove ghosting and transparency artifacts, clean up the blended areas."

findings.claim: Auto white balance is recommended, because fixed presets (Cloudy, Shade, Tungsten) bake in a color cast. AutoHDR also says to shoot the middle exposure first, since many cameras lock white balance to the first frame of an auto-bracket sequence and the AI uses that frame as its color reference.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Many cameras lock white balance to the first frame of an auto-bracket sequence. Leading with the middle (most neutrally exposed) shot typically gives the AI the most accurate color reference for the whole set.

findings.claim: The knowledge base says the AI corrects white balance and color cast whether the camera was set to auto or a custom white balance.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: the AI corrects white balance and color cast whether you shoot auto or a custom setting

findings.claim: JPEG is the top recommendation. AutoHDR says the model was trained on JPEG inputs, so RAW gives no quality difference, only bigger files and slower uploads and processing.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: JPEG is actually our top recommendation — the AI model was trained on JPEG inputs, so there's zero quality difference vs RAW.

findings.claim: Accepted inputs are JPEG; RAW in CR2, CR3, ARW, NEF, RAF, DNG, RW2, ORF, PEF and SRW; PNG, BMP, GIF and WEBP; and HEIC from iPhone. For newer cameras whose RAW files fail, the advice is to convert to JPEG and re-upload.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: AutoHDR supports JPEG and most major RAW formats including CR2, CR3, ARW, NEF, RAF, DNG, RW2, ORF, PEF, and SRW ... PNG, BMP, GIF, and WEBP ... HEIC (iPhone).

findings.claim: RAW uploads go through a RAW-to-JPEG step that fully corrects distortion and vignetting, reportedly with RawTherapee and Lensfun profiles plus embedded lens metadata. JPEG uploads are treated as already corrected, so photographers need in-camera lens correction or 'Apply Lens Profile' turned on in their export.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: distortion and vignetting are fully corrected during the RAW-to-JPEG conversion step ... make sure your camera's in-body lens correction is on, or that "Apply Lens Profile" is enabled. (Search extract also attributed RawTherapee + Lensfun to this page; full text not fetched.)

findings.claim: The architecture is likely a RAW front-end (RawTherapee/Lensfun) that converts everything to 8-bit JPEG-like frames, followed by a learned fusion model trained on JPEG brackets. A clone could do the same with RawTherapee CLI or LibRaw plus Lensfun, then run fusion in display-referred sRGB rather than linear radiance.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Inference combining 'trained on JPEG inputs' (shoot-jpeg-or-raw page) with 'RAW-to-JPEG conversion step' (lens-corrections page).

findings.claim: One AutoHDR help page, as the search tool summarized it, says lens profile corrections are applied to every upload and cannot be disabled. That conflicts with the FAQ saying JPEGs are not lens-corrected. The exact wording could not be checked.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Lens profile corrections are applied automatically to every upload and cannot be disabled. (search extract; attribution to this exact page uncertain)

findings.claim: Brackets are grouped into sets by vision-based similarity, not timestamps. Users do not need to pre-sort, and each detected set becomes one edited output.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: vision-based grouping algorithm matches brackets by how similar the angles look — timestamps don't affect it ... each bracket set is merged into one final edited photo.

findings.claim: Grouping is purely visual, so two shots of the same angle (for example door open and door closed) or similar drone angles can be merged into one bracket set. The fixes are to delete original frames before reshooting an angle, upload drones as a separate shoot, or upload problem shots one at a time as their own shoots.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: AutoHDR groups photos using vision-based similarity rather than timestamps, so similar-angle drone shots can be merged into a bracket set ... upload them one at a time as individual shoots ... shoot from clearly distinct positions, elevations, or framing.

findings.claim: Ambient and flash brackets of the same angle can look different enough to be grouped separately and edited one by one, which gives poor results. There is no documented self-service regroup tool; the user sends the shoot link to support for review.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: ambient and flash brackets look so different from each other that they get grouped as separate exposures and edited individually ... if your output shows two photos where there should be one merged result, send us the shoot link.

findings.claim: The over-merge and under-merge failures suggest grouping clusters frames on exposure-invariant visual features (embeddings or keypoint matches) under a similarity threshold, with no EXIF time, EV or sequence constraint. A flash frame changes the appearance enough to fall below the threshold, while different scenes from nearly the same viewpoint pass it.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Inference from documented failure modes on does-autohdr-auto-merge-hdr-brackets, drone-shots-treated-as-brackets, and recommended-photography-settings (duplicate angles merged).

findings.claim: A separate Deduplication step, which can be switched off in Style Settings, removes near-duplicate photos. Together with merging during grouping, this is a documented reason users get fewer final photos than they uploaded. Missing files from Dropbox or integrations are another.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Deduplication removes similar angles and reduces the output count. If you want every input preserved, turn it off ... similar brackets are identified through vision-based grouping and merged before the HDR blending process.

findings.claim: Single exposures are processed with no bracket blending, but corrections, sky replacement and any enabled add-ons still apply. Daytime single shots get standard interior or exterior processing, chosen automatically.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Single exposures don't benefit from bracket blending, but the AI still applies corrections, sky replacement, and any add-ons you have enabled ... The AI applies standard exterior or interior processing depending on the shot.

findings.claim: Photos already shot at twilight or night need the 'Twilight' model chosen from a dropdown when naming the shoot. It costs 5 credits per photo and needs no bracket. Virtual Twilight (day-to-dusk conversion) costs 5 credits to generate plus 1 to download, 6 in total.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Virtual Twilight has two separate steps — 5 credits for the AI to generate the conversion, then 1 credit to download the final photo, for 6 credits total.

findings.claim: Aerials can be uploaded in the same shoot as interiors; the AI separates single-exposure aerials from interior brackets. Aerials often finish before interiors. Sky Replacement is on for aerials by default and can be turned off per upload or in Style Settings for mountain or landscape scenes.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: the AI automatically separates interior brackets from single-exposure aerials ... Sky Replacement is on for aerials by default ... toggle Sky Replacement off for that upload, or adjust the setting at autohdr.com/account under Style Settings.

findings.claim: A Spiro user said sky replacement fails when clouds cover mountains and cannot be turned off from the Spiro photographer portal. Their workaround is to upload those jobs to AutoHDR manually. The request was 'In Review' when indexed.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: asks for photographers to be able to disable sky replacement within AutoHDR from the Spiro Photographer portal ... team currently marks those jobs and uploads them to AutoHDR manually.

findings.claim: These toggles live under autohdr.com/account → Style Settings: Perspective Correction (on by default, straightens verticals, applies a slight crop); Sky Replacement (on by default); Declutter (opt-in, 1 credit per photo); Deduplication; Auto Fire and Auto TV Screen Replacement (applied during processing and baked in, so undoing them means re-uploading); and TV Screen Replacement 'Custom' with a user-uploaded image.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Declutter is opt-in (1 credit per photo when on) ... Perspective Correction — turn off for wide-angle buildings ... Auto Fire and Auto TV Screen Replacement ... bake into the output, so removing them after the fact requires re-uploading.

findings.claim: Because perspective correction crops slightly, the guide says to leave buffer space at the top and bottom of the frame, and to turn it off for extreme angles or upward shots of tall buildings. The change applies only to new uploads and re-uploads.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Leave buffer space at the top and bottom of the frame. Perspective Correction applies a slight crop, and important details at the edges can get cut off.

findings.claim: There are two named base styles. 'Classic' is the industry-standard HDR look; 'Lisa' adds more 'pop' with much deeper window pulls. The default is set in Style Settings, alongside global sliders for brightness, contrast, vibrance and white balance, plus custom Interior and Exterior profiles.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Classic ... the "gold standard" industry style used by most companies ... Lisa ... extra "pop" with much deeper window pulls.

findings.claim: AI Re-Edit is a text-prompt editing tool that can also take a reference photo. It is free for the first 3 images per shoot and 1 credit per image after that. Regenerations are free. Re-uploading or re-running a shoot is free, since billing happens only at download.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: The AI re-edit tool is free for the first three images per shoot, then costs one credit per re-edit after that ... generally not more than three errors per shoot.

findings.claim: Manual tools after processing are a Basic Adjustments tab (Lightroom-style brightness, shadows, highlights, contrast, and per-color HSL), a Repaint tool that targets a surface with a hex color, AutoFill (mask plus prompt, free), and a 'View Inputs' button that shows the original brackets for a merged output.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Basic Adjustments gives you Lightroom-style control ... AI Re-Edit ... accepts a reference photo to edit toward a specific style. (Repaint/View Inputs from colors-not-realistic-accurate; AutoFill from autohdr-removed-lamps-fixtures)

findings.claim: A shoot of about 40 output photos averages about 15 minutes to process. Dropbox, Spiro and other integrations add a 20-minute wait after the last file arrives. Website uploads not back after 15+ minutes have probably failed; staff monitor for failed shoots 24/7 and re-run them.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Average processing time for a shoot of around 40 edited output photos is about 15 minutes ... AutoHDR waits 20 minutes after your last file upload before kicking off the shoot.

findings.claim: Dropbox automation needs the root folder /AutoHDR/, then an address folder, then an input folder named exactly '01-RAW-Photos'. Names are case- and punctuation-sensitive ('01 RAW Photos' and '01-raw-photos' both fail). Processing starts after a 20-minute quiet period, and files that arrive late go into the next window and are added to the same listing.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: AutoHDR waits 20 minutes after the last detected upload before triggering ... just upload the missing photos to the same 01-RAW-Photos folder ... the new edited results are added to the same existing listing automatically.

findings.claim: Finished photos appear at autohdr.com/listings, an email goes out when processing ends, and for Dropbox users the files are written to /AutoHDR/<address>/04-FINALS-Photos. Aryeo works only through Dropbox; HD PhotoHub, Tonomo and Spiro have direct integrations.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: automatically creates a 04-FINALS-Photos folder inside the same address folder in your Dropbox, alongside the 01-RAW-Photos folder you uploaded to.

findings.claim: There is no MLS-size or multi-size download option. Photos come back in the same dimensions and format they were uploaded in, and the FAQ points users to an outside tool (Squoosh) to resize.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Currently, AutoHDR returns photos in the same dimensions and format they were uploaded in, with no built-in option to download at multiple sizes.

findings.claim: Output file naming and walkthrough order are set under Style Settings. Options include the business name or the shoot name plus numbers; room-type tagging sorts images by a configurable room order. As of April 2026, custom names apply only to web-UI uploads, not integrations.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Tags images by room type and reorders them in your preferred sequence ... As of April 2026, custom file names only apply to uploads done in the web UI directly on autohdr.com.

findings.claim: Browser uploads need no software and work on desktop or mobile (camera roll or SD adapter); AutoHDR advises one listing per upload. Uploads and exports are kept for 7 days, then archived and deleted. Uploading and previewing are free, and Free, Standard and Basic plan previews carry a watermark until a credit is spent.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: AutoHDR stores your uploaded images and final exports for 7 days. After that, the project is archived and all photos are deleted from our servers ... Uploading and previewing are always free.

findings.claim: The pricing model is 1 credit per downloaded photo. A free plan gives 10 photos a month, pay-as-you-go top-ups are available, and plan credits roll over month to month.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Pay per photo by topping up credits at autohdr.com/pricing ... the free plan includes 10 photos/month at no cost ... credits roll over month to month.

findings.claim: In a 2026 Fred Miranda forum thread, two users reported that AutoHDR output looked good at fit-to-screen but soft or mushy at 100%, with fine texture lost. A third user found sharpness acceptable on 5 tripod-shot interiors.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: the AI result looked great at first, but once I zoomed in, a lot of the fine detail and texture was gone.

findings.claim: Softness at 100% fits a generative or learned fusion model that runs at reduced resolution and is then upscaled or guided back to full size, rather than a classical per-pixel exposure fusion. This is a hypothesis and needs testing on sample outputs.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Inference from user reports of soft/mushy detail plus vendor statement that output dimensions match input.

findings.topic: exposure fusion (Mertens 2007): reference implementation in OpenCV
findings.claim: OpenCV's MergeMertens (cites MK07, Mertens/Kautz/Van Reeth, Pacific Graphics 2007, pp. 382-390) does not need exposure times and outputs an LDR image directly in [0..1], with no tonemapping step. Debevec and Robertson need exposure times as float32 seconds and produce 32-bit float HDR that must then be tonemapped.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: "an alternative approach called exposure fusion (Mertens), that produces low dynamic range image and does not need the exposure times data" ... "we do not need to use any tonemap algorithm because the Mertens algorithm already gives us the result in the range of [0..1]."

findings.claim: In OpenCV merge.cpp, Mertens weights are contrast × saturation × well-exposedness. Contrast is |Laplacian| of grayscale. Saturation is sqrt(sum of squared deviations of R,G,B from their mean), with no division by the channel count. Well-exposedness is the product over channels of exp(-(c-0.5)^2/0.08), i.e. a Gaussian with sigma 0.2 centred on 0.5. A 1e-12 epsilon is added, weights are normalised per pixel, and images are blended with Laplacian pyramids of floor(log2(min(W,H))) levels.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Mat expo = splitted[c] - 0.5f; pow(expo, 2.0f, expo); expo = -expo / 0.08f; exp(expo, expo); ... Laplacian(gray, contrast, CV_32F); contrast = abs(contrast); ... weights[i] = weights[i].mul(wellexp) + 1e-12f; ... int maxlevel = static_cast<int>(logf(...min(size.width, size.height)) / logf(2.0f));

findings.topic: exposure fusion: OpenCV default weights differ from the paper and from enfuse
findings.claim: OpenCV's createMergeMertens defaults are contrast_weight=1.0, saturation_weight=1.0 and exposure_weight=0.0, so well-exposedness is OFF by default. The enfuse defaults (as mirrored in the PyImageFuser GUI) are exposure 1.0, saturation 0.2, contrast 0, entropy 0, exposure-optimum 0.5 and exposure-width 0.2, with up to 29 pyramid levels. A clone has to pick its own weights explicitly. Results from 'OpenCV Mertens' and 'enfuse' will differ noticeably.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: CV_EXPORTS_W Ptr<MergeMertens> createMergeMertens(float contrast_weight = 1.0f, float saturation_weight = 1.0f, float exposure_weight = 0.0f); | PyImageFuser ui_layout.py: OpenCV tab sliders default exposure 0.0 '# enfuse 1.0', saturation 1.0 '# enfuse 0.2', contrast 1.0 '# enfuse 0'; Enfuse tab: exposure_optimum 0.5, exposure_width 0.2, levels range 1-29 default 29 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hvdwolf/PyImageFuser/HEAD/ui_layout.py)

findings.claim: OpenCV implements Debevec-Malik as CalibrateDebevec (defaults samples=70, lambda=10.0, random=false; grid sampling of pixel locations; lambda is the smoothness weight) plus MergeDebevec. MergeDebevec computes a weighted average of log radiance (g(Z) - ln t) with a hat/triangle weight that peaks at mid-range (epsilon 1e-6 at the ends), then exponentiates. The paper reference is Debevec & Malik, 'Recovering high dynamic range radiance maps from photographs'.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Mat triangleWeights(int length) { // hat function ... w.at<float>(0) = epsilon; ... (i < half) ? i : (maxVal - i) } | createCalibrateDebevec(int samples = 70, float lambda = 10.0f, bool random = false) | paper URL per opencv.bib: https://www.pauldebevec.com/Research/HDR/debevec-siggraph97.pdf

findings.claim: OpenCV's Robertson method (Robertson, Borman, Stevenson, ICIP 1999, 'Dynamic range improvement through multiple exposures') estimates the response iteratively: CalibrateRobertson uses a Gauss-Seidel solver with max_iter=30 and threshold=0.01. The weights are a Gaussian-like bump, scale*exp(-(i/q-2)^2)+shift with q=(len-1)/4. The merge is result = sum(t_i * w * im) / sum(t_i^2 * w), starting from a linear response.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: float q = (length - 1) / 4.0f; float e4 = exp(4.f); float scale = e4/(e4 - 1.f); ... value = scale*exp(-value * value) + shift; | merge.cpp: result += times.at<float>((int)i) * w.mul(im); wsum += times^2 * w; | createCalibrateRobertson(int max_iter = 30, float threshold = 0.01f)

findings.claim: OpenCV AlignMTB implements Ward's 2003 median-threshold-bitmap registration (J. Graphics Tools 8(2)) for hand-held exposures. Defaults are max_bits=6 (shift search up to about 63 px), exclude_range=4 (noise exclusion around the median) and cut=true (crop instead of zero-fill). It is translation-only, so it does not handle rotation, parallax or moving objects. Those need homography/flow or learned deghosting.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: createAlignMTB(int max_bits = 6, int exclude_range = 4, bool cut = true); max_bits: log2 of max shift, 5 or 6 usually enough (31 or 63 pixels); cut: 'if true cuts images, otherwise fills the new regions with zeros.' (Translation-only is my characterization of MTB, not quoted.)

It has 3 LDR .tif exposures per scene, and its test set is 15 scenes (from EXTRA and PAPER). The full dataset is about 8 GB. The reimplementations offer three merge architectures: direct, WE (weight estimator) and WIE (weight and image estimator).

findings.topic: ghost-free HDR: AHDRNet (Yan et al. CVPR 2019)
findings.claim: AHDRNet ('Attention-guided Network for Ghost-free HDR Imaging') has NO license file, so default copyright applies and it is not safe for commercial reuse. It uses PyTorch 0.3.1 and Python 2.7, with MATLAB for data prep. Defaults are nChannel=6 (each frame as LDR RGB plus its HDR-domain RGB), nFeat=64 and growthRate=32. Attention modules compare frames 1 and 3 against the middle reference frame (3 inputs). A pretrained model is in ./trained-model.

findings.claim: Homedeck (GitHub org: 'Automated image editing for real estate photography', homedeck.io, USA) open-sourced 'Deep-Fusion: Deep Bilateral Learning for Multiple Exposure Fusion' under Apache-2.0 (archived Nov 2021). v1: a CNN over the stacked 3-exposure input builds a bilateral grid of per-exposure weights (default exposure_count=3, grid 64x64x32). A 1x1-conv guide map slices it with torch grid_sample, so it is pure PyTorch and CPU-runnable. Output is the weighted sum of exposures. v2: each exposure is resized to 512, splatted to a 16-bin grid and sliced, and weights are softmax-normalised. Training pairs (bracket stack to fused target) use 512 px patches, with contrast and saturation losses taken 'from Mertens et al.'. This is strong evidence that real-estate AI HDR vendors use learned per-pixel fusion weights, not radiance-map HDR.

findings.claim: Image-Adaptive-3DLUT is Apache-2.0. A small CNN sees a 256x256 downscale and predicts 3 weights that blend 3 learned basis LUTs of 33^3 (one initialised to identity, two to zero) into one image-specific LUT. findings.topic: automatic upright / perspective correction (ShiftN-style, darktable ashift)
findings.claim: darktable's 'rotate and perspective' module (GPL-3) is a mature open recipe for automatic verticals. Line segments come from LSD (gamma 0.45 applied first, min line length 5 px). Lines are classified as vertical or horizontal converging sets. RANSAC rejects outliers (400 runs, about 60% elimination ratio), and Nelder-Mead (400 iterations) fits rotation (default range ±10°), vertical/horizontal lens shift (±1.0) and shear (±0.2). At least 2 lines are needed. It assumes a 28 mm full-frame focal length when EXIF is missing. Auto-crop is either 'largest area' or 'original format' (keep aspect ratio). The docs note that correcting verticals to only 80-90% can look more natural.

findings.topic: lens distortion models and profile database (Lensfun)
findings.claim: Lensfun ships the standard radial distortion models. poly3: r_d = r_u(1 - k1 + k1 r_u^2). poly5: r_d = r_u(1 + k1 r_u^2 + k2 r_u^4). ptlens (also Hugin's): r_d = r_u(a r_u^3 + b r_u^2 + c r_u + 1 - a - b - c). It also has Adobe Camera Model (ACM). The libraries are LGPL-3, the apps GPL-3 and the lens database CC BY-SA 3.0. For a plumb-line self-calibration you fit k1 (or a,b,c) so that detected long straight segments become straight. The parameter count stays tiny, so a CPU fit is cheap. (The plumb-line fitting step is my inference; this repo provides the models, not the calibration.)

findings.claim: Background knowledge, not fetched: 'flambient' = flash + ambient. The photographer shoots ambient frame(s) (often bracketed) plus one or more flash frames (on-camera bounced or off-camera) from a tripod. In Photoshop the flash frame supplies neutral colour and clean shadows and the ambient supplies natural light falloff, typically by layering the flash frame in 'Luminosity' or 'Color' blend mode, or masking it, over the ambient. A separate exterior exposure fills the windows. Implication: an AI HDR service that accepts a 'flash' frame needs per-frame role detection (ambient vs flash vs window), e.g. from EXIF flash-fired tags or exposure.

findings.claim: Background knowledge, not fetched: a manual 'window pull' takes the frame exposed for the exterior (darkest usable bracket, sometimes lit with flash), layers it over the interior base, and masks it to the window panes. findings.claim: Hypothesis from the literature above. A real-estate AI HDR service most plausibly runs: (1) RAW/JPEG ingest and bracket grouping by EXIF time and exposure; (2) global alignment (MTB, ECC or homography); (3) learned per-pixel fusion weights in a low-res bilateral-grid style (Deep-Fusion/HDRNet) applied at full resolution, or Mertens-style fusion with a learned prior; (4) global parametric retouch predicted by a CNN (tone curve, WB temperature/tint, selective colour), or an image-adaptive 3D LUT; (5) semantic masks (window, sky) for window pull and sky replacement; (6) line-based vertical correction plus a lens profile or plumb-line model; (7) resize/export for MLS. Most steps are CPU-feasible at listing resolutions except heavy segmentation backbones.
